title: Adani Enterprises Pays $275 Million to Settle Iran Sanctions Charges — What It Means for the Group's US Ambitions
excerpt: The OFAC settlement over mislabelled Iranian LPG shipments caps a turbulent legal chapter, even as Gautam Adani doubles down on a $10 billion American investment pledge
body:
The Adani Group's flagship company has agreed to pay $275 million to the United States Treasury to settle allegations that it violated American sanctions on Iran — a resolution that closes one of several legal fronts the Indian conglomerate has been battling, while raising fresh questions about governance at one of Asia's largest business empires.

The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC), the Treasury's sanctions enforcement arm, identified 32 apparent violations by Adani Enterprises involving the purchase of liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) shipments that originated from Iran. According to the settlement document, Adani Enterprises bought the LPG from a Dubai-based trader who claimed the gas came from Oman and Iraq. Internal company documents and shipping records, however, indicated the cargo was Iranian in origin.

The transactions in question spanned from November 2023 to June 2025 and totalled approximately $192.1 million in value processed through American financial institutions — a critical detail, because routing payments through the US banking system brings foreign companies squarely under OFAC's jurisdiction regardless of where the physical goods are loaded or delivered.

Adani Enterprises initially dismissed reports of the probe as "baseless," telling investors in regulatory filings that it did not handle Iranian cargo and was unaware of any US investigation. The Wall Street Journal first reported the OFAC inquiry in late 2024, noting that US prosecutors were examining whether Adani-linked entities had imported Iranian LPG through the company's Mundra port in Gujarat.

The company later acknowledged the investigation and said it had "voluntarily engaged" with OFAC, discontinued all LPG imports in June 2025, and noted the business line accounted for just 1.46 per cent of annual revenue. The $275 million settlement — roughly 143 per cent of the underlying transaction value — represents one of the larger OFAC penalties involving an Indian company and signals Washington's willingness to enforce Iran sanctions against major emerging-market conglomerates.

The OFAC settlement arrives alongside the resolution of a separate Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) civil lawsuit alleging that Gautam Adani and associates paid hundreds of millions of dollars in bribes to Indian government officials to secure solar energy contracts. The SEC case, filed in late 2024 as part of a broader federal indictment, is reportedly heading toward a consent decree. Criminal fraud charges against Adani personally may be dropped, according to multiple reports, as part of what legal observers describe as a diplomatic recalibration following Adani's pledge to invest $10 billion in US energy and infrastructure projects.

For the Indian diaspora — many of whom hold Adani Group stocks directly or through Indian mutual fund portfolios — the settlement carries a dual message. On one hand, it removes a cloud of uncertainty: Adani Enterprises shares had fallen 2–2.5 per cent when the OFAC probe was first reported, and the definitive resolution of sanctions liability could stabilise sentiment. On the other hand, the sheer size of the fine and the pattern of initial denial followed by quiet cooperation underscores governance concerns that Hindenburg Research's 2023 short-seller report first thrust into the global spotlight.

NRI investors with exposure to Adani Group stocks — whether through direct holdings, thematic ETFs, or Indian index funds where Adani companies carry meaningful weight — should note that while the legal risk is diminishing, reputational risk lingers. The group's ability to execute its US investment plan, and whether American partners and regulators treat the settlements as a clean slate, will likely determine the next phase of the stock's trajectory.

The LPG business itself is now defunct, but the case is a reminder that for Indian conglomerates operating across geopolitical fault lines, compliance infrastructure is no longer optional — it is existential.
